title: AI in Education #13: Five Things I Learned from Joe Liemandt about Motivation, Data, and the Future of the Teaching Profession
author: Craig Barton
source: Mr Barton Maths / Craig Barton (eedi.substack.com), September 1, 2026
summary: The thirteenth installment of Craig Barton's "AI in Education" interview series covers a conversation with Joe Liemandt, the software entrepreneur who became principal of Alpha School, the US AI-powered school where students spend two hours a day on adaptive apps with "Guides" instead of subject-specialist teachers. Barton is careful to flag upfront that Alpha's performance claims come from internal, unverified, and contested analyses, then extracts five takeaways regardless. Liemandt's central claim is that motivation, not software quality, explains roughly 90% of Alpha's results — citing Laurence Holt's "5% problem" (many EdTech products only show gains once you exclude the 95% of students who don't meaningfully engage) and describing Alpha's afternoon privileges (sports, projects) as the actual engine that makes the morning academic work happen. Other takeaways include Alpha's "100 for 100" program that pays students $100 per grade level of test mastery to motivate remedial catch-up without the stigma of being told they're behind grade level, and Liemandt's argument that Alpha's tightly closed instructional loop generates the kind of fine-grained measurement learning science has never had, comparable to the invention of the microscope in biology. Liemandt predicts there will be more teachers in twenty years, not fewer, but is explicit that he won't call Alpha's adults "teachers" because they don't deliver academic instruction — a distinction Barton presses him on, since it implies the specific pleasure of explaining one's subject, which drew many teachers into the profession, may not survive the model's spread.
points: Liemandt attributes roughly 90% of Alpha's success to motivation rather than software quality, citing Laurence Holt's "5% problem": many EdTech products only show positive results once you exclude the 95% of students who don't meaningfully engage with the product.

Alpha's "100 for 100" program pays students $100 for scoring 100% on a test several grade levels below their age, then $100 again for the next grade level up, motivating remedial catch-up by rewarding rate of learning rather than exposing students to the stigma of a fixed grade-level label.

Liemandt argues Alpha's tightly closed instructional loop — knowing whether a lesson was delivered as designed, whether the student was attentive, whether prerequisites were met, and whether understanding was actually checked — is the fine-grained measurement instrument learning science has lacked for forty years, comparable to the microscope's effect on biology.

Alpha's internal data suggests that for children roughly 9-12, most problems aren't hard enough to require worked examples and repeated practice suffices, but that arriving at algebra without worked-example instruction is, in Liemandt's words, fatal to learning.

Liemandt predicts more teachers in twenty years, not fewer, but deliberately avoids calling Alpha's non-instructional adults "teachers" since the term would misrepresent what parents are actually buying — a distinction that implicitly concedes the explaining-your-subject part of teaching may not survive at scale.
quotes: His reasoning is about motivation, which Joe reckons explains 90% of Alpha's success. He points to Laurence Holt's 5% problem: the finding that many EdTech products' positive results are only positive when you exclude 95% of the students who fail to engage with the product.

In their online sports academy, the kids do their two hours of academics at home in the morning, and only get a QR code for the afternoon session at the athletics facility if the system says they have genuinely mastered the work. Joe's line is that if he relaxes that constraint even slightly, the mornings collapse.

Alpha set up a programme called "100 for 100" where a student sits a test several years below their age grade and gets $100 for getting 100%. Then they take the test for the next grade up, and if they get full marks, it's another $100 coming their way.
You do not tell that child they are in third grade and years behind. You tell them their rate of learning is excellent, because it is, and because that number gives them a reason to keep going.
He thinks learning science has forty-odd years of good ideas and no microscope, because the effect of any intervention is swamped by the messy classroom it happens in.

It takes roughly 11 hours in their maths facts app for a third grader to reach fluency. A fourth grader who has that fluency gets through the year's maths in about 30 hours. A fourth grader who does not takes about 61.
He will not, because if the adult is not delivering the academic instruction, the word gives parents the wrong picture of what they are buying.
